classification_profile.title: University of California Protection Levels (P1–P4)
classification_profile.description:
The four Protection Levels defined by the UC Institutional Information and IT Resource Classification Standard, IT Security Committee Item SC-0002. Read from the published Standard and nothing else: the Standard defines the levels and the classification process, while the security controls required at each level live in BFB-IS-3 Electronic Information Security and the Location implementations under it. This profile therefore states NO controls at any level — see the note on levels[].controls being absent throughout, which is the honest rendering of a source that defines levels without stating per-level controls.

An EXAMPLE, not a maintained document. Fork it, correct automat's reading against your own reading, and re-attest.

This attests to authorship of the reading and to nothing else: not that the reading is correct, not that it is complete, and not that the University of California has seen it. No signature material accompanies this attestation, and automat verifies none in v1. Re-attested at AUDIT-2 for three provenance corrections, none of which changed a claim about the policy. F5, resolved: the BFB-IS-3 citation now carries date_basis not-retrieved and no source_id, rather than retrieved-only with source_id naming a different document — the schema gained a fourth date_basis value for a citation that was never read at all, per the maintainer's decision on Q18. The claim about the policy is unchanged: BFB-IS-3 still governs and is still unread; only the machine-readable fields now say so correctly.

determination.process:
Proprietors are responsible for determining the Protection Level of Institutional Information and IT Resources under their area of responsibility. The Standard walks three steps. Step 1, evaluate the Institutional Information against seven factors: regulatory framework, business impact of a loss of confidentiality/integrity/availability, risk of harm to individuals, required Availability Level, access needs, data and system architecture, and use-case change. Step 2, select the classification level using the published classification guides and any analysis performed, and document it in the appropriate repository or system of record. Step 3, set review and retention schedules with the Records Management Policy and work with a Security SME on compensating controls and disposition. Where a data type is not in the guides, the Standard directs the Proprietor to consult their Privacy Officer, Compliance Officer or CISO, and permits consulting Location legal resources, the Office of the President Office of General Counsel, or other subject matter experts.

Go and ask the Proprietor for the Institutional Information in question. There is no step in this process that a tool performs.

citation.section: Section 4.2 Classifying Institutional Information, Steps 1–3 (pages 7–10); Section 6 Appendix A – Roles and Responsibilities (page 14)
citation.quote: Proprietors must comply with this Standard and are responsible for determining the Protection Levels for Institutional Information and IT Resources under their area of responsibility.

citation.section: Section 4.2 Classifying Institutional Information, Step 2, item 2 (page 10)
citation.quote: Proprietors may use the published Protection Level in the guide or raise it based on the specific use case, but they cannot lower it without going through the exception process described in IS-3, III.2.2, “Exception Process.”

determination.notes:
The asymmetry is the source's, stated in one sentence: a Proprietor may raise the published Protection Level on a use case but may not lower it outside the named exception process. The same sentence goes on to say that the AVAILABILITY Level may be raised or lowered on use case — an axis this profile does not model; see unmodeled_axes.

The named exception process lives in BFB-IS-3, a document this profile has NOT retrieved or hashed. It is recorded here as the process the Standard names, cited to the Standard, and no claim is made about what IS-3 III.2.2 says.

levels.label: P1 – Minimal
levels.definition: Public information or information intended to be readily obtainable by the public, but whose integrity is important and for which unauthorized modification is the primary protection concern. IT Resources for which the application of minimum security requirements is sufficient. The source's one-word gloss for this level is "Public".

citation.section: Section 3.1 Protection Levels, P1 – Minimal row (page 5–6)
citation.quote: Public information or information intended to be readily obtainable by the public, but whose integrity is important and for which unauthorized modification is the primary protection concern.

levels.label: P2 – Low
levels.definition: Institutional Information and related IT Resources that may not be specifically protected by statute, regulations or other contractual obligations or mandates, but are generally not intended for public use or access. In addition, information of which unauthorized use, access, disclosure, acquisition, modification or loss could result in minor damage or small financial loss, or cause minor impact on the privacy of an individual or group. The source's one-word gloss for this level is "Internal".

citation.section: Section 3.1 Protection Levels, P2 – Low row (page 5)
citation.quote: Institutional Information and related IT Resources that may not be specifically protected by statute, regulations or other contractual obligations or mandates, but are generally not intended for public use or access.

examples: Routine email not containing P3 or P4 information
Calendar information not containing P3 or P4 information
Meeting notes not containing P3 or P4 information

levels.label: P3 – Moderate
levels.definition: Institutional Information and related IT Resources whose unauthorized disclosure or modification could result in small to moderate fines, penalties or civil actions. Institutional Information of which unauthorized use, access, disclosure, acquisition, modification, loss or deletion could result in moderate damage to UC, its students, patients, research subjects, employees, community and/or reputation related to a breach or compromise; could have a moderate impact on the privacy of a group; could result in moderate financial loss; or could require legal action. This classification level also includes lower risk items that, when combined, represent increased risk. The source's one-word gloss for this level is "Proprietary".

citation.section: Section 3.1 Protection Levels, P3 – Moderate row (pages 4–5)
citation.quote: This classification level also includes lower risk items that, when combined, represent increased risk.

examples: Certain types of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) – not classified as P4
Building entry records from automated card key system
Research results and supporting data from a long-term study (not containing P4 information)
Medical devices supporting diagnostics not containing P4 information

levels.label: P4 – High
levels.definition: Institutional Information and related IT Resources whose unauthorized disclosure or modification could result in significant fines, penalties, regulatory action, or civil or criminal violations. Statutory, regulatory and contract obligations are major drivers for this risk level. Other drivers include, but are not limited to: the risk of significant harm or impairment to UC students, patients, research subjects, employees, guests/program participants, UC reputation related to a breach or compromise, the overall operation of the Location or essential services. The source's one-word gloss for this level is "Statutory".

citation.section: Section 3.1 Protection Levels, P4 – High row (page 4)
citation.quote: Institutional Information and related IT Resources whose unauthorized disclosure or modification could result in significant fines, penalties, regulatory action, or civil or criminal violations.

examples: Certain types of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) – large collections or special sensitivity to privacy
Human subject research data with individual identifiers
Industrial Control Systems affecting life and safety
levels.notes: The source's examples at this level name several external regimes by their subject matter — protected health information, credit card data, Controlled Unclassified Information. They are recorded above as examples, which is what the source calls them, and NOT as external_obligations entries: the Standard names data types the Proprietor may recognize, it does not state that a regime applies at this level. Reading a routing rule into an example list would be automat concluding that a regime applies, which is the operator's declaration to make.

composition.statement: If Institutional Information with higher Protection and/or Availability Levels also contains some lower-level information, the Institutional Information must be secured to meet the requirements of the highest Protection Level.

citation.section: Section 4.2 Classifying Institutional Information, Step 1, item 5 Access needs (page 9)
citation.quote: If Institutional Information with higher Protection and/or Availability Levels also contains some lower-level information, the Institutional Information must be secured to meet the requirements of the highest Protection Level.

citation.section: Section 4.2 Classifying Institutional Information, Step 2, items 2 and 3 (page 10)
citation.quote: Proprietors must document the classification in the appropriate repository or system of record.

over_classification.note: Raising is permitted on the specific use case and the resulting classification must be documented in a system of record. The Standard states the documentation requirement for every classification decision rather than for raised ones specifically; it is recorded as required here because a raised level is a classification decision.

unmodeled_axes.name: Availability Level (A1–A4)
unmodeled_axes.statement:
The Standard classifies Institutional Information and IT Resources on TWO independent axes: Protection Level P1–P4, based on the level of concern related to confidentiality and integrity, and Availability Level A1–A4, based on the business impact a loss of availability or service would have. This profile models the Protection axis only, because a Protection Level is what an account is rated for.

Recorded rather than omitted, and the disclosure is the point. To a reader who knows this Standard, a profile showing four levels and no availability axis looks like an incomplete transcription; to a reader who does not, it looks as though UC classified on one axis. The two axes are also not parallel in the one place it matters most: a Proprietor may not lower a Protection Level outside the exception process, but the Standard says explicitly that a Proprietor MAY select a lower Availability Level than the guide specifies. An implementation that treated the availability axis as another instance of this one would carry that permission across, and be wrong in the permissive direction.

citation.section: Section 3.2 Availability Levels (page 6); Section 4.2 Step 1, item 4 Required Availability Level (page 8)
citation.quote: Unlike Protection Level, Proprietors may choose to select a lower Availability Level than what is specified in the guide.

citations.title: UC Institutional Information and IT Resource Classification Standard
citations.note:
Dated by the “Last Updated: 8/21/2019” stamp in the document's own page footer, which is why date_basis is last-updated-in-document rather than published-effective-date. The revision history records a later event — “10/3/19 … Approved by ITLC” — and that approval date is NOT used as the effective date here: the Standard's own footer is what the document presents as its date on every page, and choosing the later of two dates a document states would be automat picking which one counts.

The URI is the classification policy page the Standard's Step 2 names as where the classification guides can be found; the PDF hashed in sources[] was retrieved from that page's document link.

citations.title: UC Electronic Information Security (BFB-IS-3)
citations.note:
NOT RETRIEVED. The parent policy the Standard says drives it, and the document holding the exception process the Standard names. Recorded because a reader of this profile needs to know it exists and that this profile has not read it. Retrieval was attempted and failed with a TLS error. NO claim in this profile is sourced to IS-3 itself — the exception-process reference under determination.may_lower is cited to the Standard's own sentence naming it, and that citation's source_id points at the Standard (uc-classification-standard), which is the only document hashed here. Every checkable claim in this profile still traces to bytes somebody can verify.

date_basis is not-retrieved, added at AUDIT-2 F5's resolution: the prior draft recorded this citation as retrieved-only with source_id naming the Standard, because the schema had no fourth value for "never read" and the validator required a source_id on the only basis available that forbade an effective_date. That made both machine-readable fields wrong — retrieved-only asserts bytes were read and found dateless, and this document's bytes were never fetched at all; source_id pointed a re-verifier at a hash that is not IS-3's. not-retrieved forbids both fields, so their absence now means exactly what the prose says instead of contradicting it.

policy_caveat: automat encodes a technical reading of published policy. It is not legal advice and not a compliance determination. The agreement, award terms, or contract clause your institution signed governs; your sponsored programs office, contracts office, or counsel decides what applies and which revision. Where policy is ambiguous — for example the NIH 800-171 revision question — automat records the operator's declaration rather than resolving it. Policy citations carry effective dates and change; verify against the primary source before relying on them.

sources.title: UC Institutional Information and IT Resource Classification Standard
sources.version: IT Security Committee Item SC-0002, Last Updated 8/21/2019
sources.note:
14 pages, read in full. The hash is over the PDF bytes as retrieved, not over extracted text: a hash whose input nobody can reproduce is decoration — and this uri is now the PDF's own, so the bytes the hash covers are fetchable from the field that records where they came from. It previously named the .html policy page while media_type said application/pdf, so the one field a re-verifier needs pointed at a page rather than at a document (AUDIT-2 F6). The hash itself was correct and is unchanged: re-fetching the PDF at the uri now recorded reproduces e36e44a7 exactly, which is how the finding was resolved rather than assumed. The citation's own uri stays the policy page, because that is what the Standard's Step 2 names as where the classification guides are found.

What this document does NOT contain, so that its absence is not read as coverage: no per-level security controls, which is why every level in this profile omits `controls` rather than carrying an empty array. The Standard defines the levels and the classification process and defers controls to BFB-IS-3. It also references separate Institutional Information and Availability classification guides, and an ISO 27002:2013 / NIST CSF 1.1 section cross-reference in Section 5; none of those has been retrieved, and nothing is claimed from them.
